name: CT Roll-N-Lock Rope Clamp and Pulley
title: CT Roll-N-Lock Rope Clamp with Pulley
h1: CT Roll-N-Lock Rope Clamp and Pulley
meta: The CT Roll-N-Lock combines a rope clamp and pulley in one unit for progress capture and haul systems. What it does, where it fits on a job, and typical price.
tagline: Rope clamp and pulley in one unit for progress capture and hauling.
summary: The CT Roll-N-Lock from Climbing Technology puts a toothed rope clamp and a pulley sheave in one compact body. Climbers use it for progress capture, short haul systems, and as a rope grab that runs smoothly when the line is pulled through.
highlights: Compact enough to live on the saddle
Useful for rescue and gear-haul setups

p: The Roll-N-Lock pairs a cam with teeth and a small pulley wheel. Rope runs over the wheel one way with low friction, and the cam bites when the rope tries to run back. That makes it a self-contained progress-capture pulley, which is the heart of most simple haul systems.

On a tree job that might mean hauling a heavy saw or a bag of rigging up to a climber, building a quick mechanical advantage to tension a line, or keeping an aerial rescue setup simple. Some climbers also carry it as a backup rope grab for their SRS system. It saves carrying a separate pulley and ascender, which keeps the saddle lighter.

Read the manufacturer's instructions for this device and confirm the rope diameter and construction you climb on falls inside its approved range. A device that grips well on one rope can slip or bind on another, so test it low and slow on new rope before you trust it at height.

Inspect the cam teeth, springs, side plates, and attachment points before every climb, and keep the device free of sap and grit. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers. Never improvise a configuration the maker does not show. Compare other options in ascent and descent gear.

faq.q: Can the Roll-N-Lock be used as a climbing ascender?
faq.a: It is a rope clamp, so it can capture progress, but only use it in the configurations Climbing Technology approves for your rope and setup.

faq.q: Is it good for hauling gear?
faq.a: Yes. The pulley and clamp together make a light progress-capture point for hauling saws and rigging gear.

name: ISC Rocker Rope Grab
title: ISC Rocker Rope Grab for Arborist Climbing
meta: The ISC Rocker is a compact cam rope grab used for lanyard adjustment and progress capture in arborist systems. How it works, setup tips, and typical price.
tagline: Compact cam rope grab for lanyards and progress capture.
summary: The ISC Rocker is a compact rope grab built around a pivoting cam. Arborists use it to adjust positioning lanyards and to capture progress, and it can be clipped in or removed without untying the rope.
highlights: Made by ISC in the UK

p: The Rocker is a cam rope grab that rocks onto the rope when loaded and releases when you take the load off. That simple action makes it a tidy way to shorten a flipline or positioning lanyard: slide it up to tighten, and lean back to lock it in place.

Climbers also set it up for progress capture in a pulley system or as part of a foot-lock or chest setup, depending on what ISC approves. Because it loads onto the rope without threading the end, you can add it partway through a climb. The small size keeps it out of the way on the saddle bridge.

Read the manufacturer's instructions for this device and confirm the rope diameter and construction you climb on falls inside its approved range. A device that grips well on one rope can slip or bind on another, so test it low and slow on new rope before you trust it at height.

Inspect the cam teeth, springs, side plates, and attachment points before every climb, and keep the device free of sap and grit. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers. Never improvise a configuration the maker does not show. Compare other options in ascent and descent gear.

faq.q: What rope works in the ISC Rocker?
faq.a: Check the diameter and rope types marked on the device and in ISC's instructions. Test on your own rope before climbing on it.

faq.q: Can I use it as a lanyard adjuster?
faq.a: Yes, that is one of its most common jobs. Set it up as ISC shows and inspect the cam before each climb.

name: ART Positioner Release Lever
title: ART Positioner Release Lever Replacement Part
meta: A replacement release lever for the ART Positioner lanyard adjuster. When to swap it, how to check the device after fitting, and the typical price.
tagline: Replacement release lever for the ART Positioner lanyard adjuster.
summary: The ART Positioner release lever is the replacement part for the handle you pull to let rope run through the Positioner. A worn, bent, or lost lever makes the adjuster hard to release smoothly, and swapping it keeps a good device in service.
highlights: Replacement part for the ART Positioner
Cheaper than replacing the whole adjuster

p: The Positioner holds your lanyard length until you pull the release lever, which lets rope feed through so you can lengthen your flipline. Over time the lever takes knocks against bark and spurs, and a bent or cracked lever can make that release jerky or stiff.

If the rest of the device is in good shape, a new lever is an inexpensive fix. Fit it only as ART describes, and if you are not sure you can install it correctly, have a competent person do it. A device that has been taken apart should be function-tested on the ground before it goes back in the tree.

Small accessories like this are easy to overlook, but they change how your hardware sits and loads. Fit it the way the maker shows, then check that the carabiner gate still opens, closes, and locks freely and that nothing rubs on the rope.

Inspect it with the rest of your kit and replace it when it splits, stretches, or no longer holds the connector in position. It is an aid, not a strength component. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers. Find related items in rope grabs.

faq.q: Does this fit other lanyard adjusters?
faq.a: It is made for the ART Positioner. Do not try to adapt it to other devices.

faq.q: Should I replace the whole Positioner instead?
faq.a: If the cam, body, or attachment points are worn or damaged, yes. The lever alone only fixes a worn or broken lever.

name: ART Positioner Lanyard Adjuster
title: ART Positioner Lanyard Adjuster
meta: The ART Positioner is a mechanical lanyard adjuster for fliplines and positioning lanyards. How it works on a climb, what to check, and its typical price.
tagline: Mechanical lanyard adjuster with a release lever for fast length changes.
summary: The ART Positioner is a mechanical adjuster for positioning lanyards and fliplines. It holds your lanyard length under load and has a release lever that lets you pay out rope smoothly when you need more length.
highlights: Popular with climbers and spur climbers

body.h: How it works on a climb
p: On a removal climb you are constantly changing lanyard length around the stem. The Positioner lets you pull slack through to shorten, then holds firm when you lean back. When you need to lengthen, pull the release lever and the rope feeds out under control instead of all at once.

That smooth release is the main reason climbers pick a mechanical adjuster over a hitch. It also stays consistent in wet or cold conditions where a friction hitch can grab differently. Set it up on a lanyard rope the device is rated for, and pair it with a good locking carabiner at the saddle.

Read the manufacturer's instructions for this device and confirm the rope diameter and construction you climb on falls inside its approved range. A device that grips well on one rope can slip or bind on another, so test it low and slow on new rope before you trust it at height.

Inspect the cam teeth, springs, side plates, and attachment points before every climb, and keep the device free of sap and grit. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers. Never improvise a configuration the maker does not show. Compare other options in rope grabs.

faq.q: What lanyard rope works with the Positioner?
faq.a: Use rope that falls inside ART's approved diameter and construction range for the device, and test it on the ground first.

faq.q: Can the release lever be replaced?
faq.a: Yes. ART sells a replacement release lever if yours is bent or broken.

name: Gibbs Klimair Bidirectional Lanyard Adjuster
title: Gibbs Klimair Bidirectional Lanyard Adjuster
meta: The Gibbs Klimair bidirectional lanyard adjuster is a mechanical way to shorten and lengthen a positioning lanyard. What it does, safety checks, typical price.
tagline: Mechanical adjuster for shortening and lengthening a positioning lanyard.
summary: The Gibbs Klimair bidirectional lanyard adjuster is a mechanical device for changing the length of a positioning lanyard in both directions. It is an alternative to a friction hitch for climbers who want consistent grip and controlled release.
highlights: Mechanical grip instead of a hitch
For work positioning on the stem

p: Bidirectional means the adjuster is built to let you both take in and pay out lanyard while it still holds you in position. On a spar or a big leader, that means you can walk your lanyard up or down the stem and change length without fighting a hitch that has bound up under load.

Mechanical adjusters also behave the same in rain, cold, and sap, which a hitch cord does not always do. The trade-off is that they are matched to a narrower range of ropes, so check what the device is built for before you buy a lanyard to go with it.

Read the manufacturer's instructions for this device and confirm the rope diameter and construction you climb on falls inside its approved range. A device that grips well on one rope can slip or bind on another, so test it low and slow on new rope before you trust it at height.

Inspect the cam teeth, springs, side plates, and attachment points before every climb, and keep the device free of sap and grit. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers. Never improvise a configuration the maker does not show. Compare other options in rope grabs.

faq.q: What does bidirectional mean on a lanyard adjuster?
faq.a: It means the device is designed to let you both shorten and lengthen the lanyard while it holds your position.

faq.q: Can I use any lanyard rope with it?
faq.a: No. Use only rope diameters and types the maker lists for the device, and test the setup low before climbing.

name: 3-IN-ONE Dry Lube with Graphite
title: 3-IN-ONE Dry Graphite Lube for Carabiner Gates
meta: 3-IN-ONE dry graphite lube keeps carabiner gates, pulleys, and hardware moving without the sticky film that holds grit. How to use it and its typical price.
tagline: Dry graphite lubricant for carabiner gates, hinges, and small hardware.
summary: 3-IN-ONE dry graphite lube is a spray lubricant that dries to a thin film instead of staying wet. Climbers use it on sticky carabiner gates and hardware because it does not leave the oily coating that collects sawdust and grit.
highlights: Good for gates, hinges, and springs
Attracts less grit than wet oil
Small can fits in a gear bag
Cheap way to fix a lazy gate

p: A carabiner gate that sticks open is a hazard, and the usual cause is sap, dust, and old grease in the hinge and lock sleeve. Clean the hardware first with warm water and a brush, let it dry fully, then apply a small amount of dry lube to the hinge, spring, and lock sleeve. Work the gate a few times and wipe off any excess.

Keep lubricant off rope contact surfaces and away from your rope, slings, and textile gear. Check the hardware maker's instructions first, since some manufacturers recommend a specific cleaner or lubricant. Graphite can mark light-colored gear, so go easy with it.
Lubrication is part of regular inspection, not a fix for damaged gear. If a gate still sticks after cleaning and lubing, or if you find cracks, burrs, or worn grooves, retire the carabiner.

Store hardware dry and away from fuel, bar oil, and battery acid in the truck, since chemicals can damage both metal and textile gear. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers. Shop auto-locking carabiners when it is time to replace a worn one.

faq.q: Why use dry lube instead of oil on carabiners?
faq.a: Wet oil holds sawdust and grit, which can make a gate sticky again. A dry film attracts less dirt.

faq.q: Can it touch my climbing rope?
faq.a: Keep it off ropes, slings, and other textiles. Apply it only to the metal mechanism and wipe away excess.

name: DMM American O Carabiner
title: DMM American O Auto-Locking Oval Carabiner
meta: The DMM American O is a symmetric oval carabiner with an auto-locking gate for pulleys, rope grabs, and arborist hardware. Uses, checks, and typical price.
tagline: Symmetric oval auto-locking carabiner for pulleys and devices.
summary: The DMM American O is a symmetric oval carabiner with an auto-locking gate. The oval shape keeps pulleys, rope grabs, and rings centered, which is why arborists use it where a device needs to sit square.
highlights: Good for pulleys and rope grabs

p: An oval carabiner has the same curve top and bottom, so whatever you clip into it settles in the middle. That matters for pulleys, rope grabs, and multi-piece setups where a D shape would let the device slide toward the gate side and load unevenly.

Ovals are slightly weaker than a D of the same material because the load sits farther from the spine, but for many arborist jobs the better device alignment is worth it. An auto-locking gate means it closes and locks every time without a second thought.

Before each climb, open the gate and let it snap shut. It should close fully and lock on its own without sticking. Look for cracks, sharp edges, grooves worn by rope, and deformation at the nose or hinge. Sap and grit are the usual cause of a lazy gate, so rinse and dry the carabiner and keep the gate mechanism clean.

Retire any carabiner that has been dropped from height onto a hard surface, shock loaded, or shows wear you cannot explain. Read the markings on the spine and confirm they meet what your system needs. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers. See more auto-locking carabiners.

faq.q: Is an oval or a D carabiner better?
faq.a: A D is stronger along the spine. An oval keeps pulleys and rope grabs centered. Pick by what you are clipping.

faq.q: Can I use it for life support?
faq.a: Only if the markings and certification on the spine meet the standard your system requires.

tagline: Auto-locking carabiner with a captive bar to hold an eye in place.
summary: The DMM Captive Eye Locksafe carabiner has a captive bar that holds a spliced eye, sling, or device in one end. With its Locksafe three-stage auto-locking gate, it is built for connections that need to stay put and stay closed.
highlights: Captive bar holds the eye in position

p: A spliced eye or sling in an ordinary carabiner can rotate and end up loading the carabiner across its minor axis, near the gate. The captive bar on this DMM traps the eye in the bottom of the carabiner so it stays aligned with the spine.

That makes it a clean choice for the end of a climbing line or a lanyard, where you want the connection to behave the same every time you clip in. The Locksafe gate needs a twist and a push to open, which helps prevent it being opened by bark or a branch rubbing past.

Before each climb, open the gate and let it snap shut. It should close fully and lock on its own without sticking. Look for cracks, sharp edges, grooves worn by rope, and deformation at the nose or hinge. Sap and grit are the usual cause of a lazy gate, so rinse and dry the carabiner and keep the gate mechanism clean.

Retire any carabiner that has been dropped from height onto a hard surface, shock loaded, or shows wear you cannot explain. Read the markings on the spine and confirm they meet what your system needs. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers. See more auto-locking carabiners.

faq.q: What is a Locksafe gate?
faq.a: It is DMM's three-stage auto-locking gate. You twist and push to open it, and it locks itself when released.

faq.q: Why use a captive eye carabiner?
faq.a: It keeps a spliced eye or sling in position so the carabiner is loaded along the spine instead of across the gate.

Good for rigging and climbing hardware

Climbers use it for pulley-based hitch tending, SRS anchor setups, and as a connector on rigging gear. The Durolock gate is an auto-locking design that closes and locks on its own. Check the strength figures on the spine before using it in a life-support system.

Look for cracks, sharp edges, grooves worn by rope, and deformation at the nose or hinge. Sap and grit are the usual cause of a lazy gate, so rinse and dry the carabiner and keep the gate mechanism clean.

faq.a: The carabiner body is the same shape. The difference is the gate's locking mechanism, so pick the action you prefer.

faq.q: Why choose a large oval?

summary: The DMM Ultra O Locksafe pairs a roomy oval body with DMM's Locksafe three-stage auto-locking gate. It holds pulleys, rope grabs, and rings centered and resists being opened by accident.

p: The Ultra O has more room inside than most ovals, so it works well when you need several items in one carabiner, such as a micro pulley and a hitch cord eye, or a ring and a sling. The symmetric shape lets those pieces settle in the middle instead of sliding toward the gate.

Locksafe is DMM's three-stage gate: twist, push up, then open. It takes a moment to learn, but it is very hard for a branch, rope, or bark to open it by accident. That is a sensible trade on a connector that sits in the middle of your climbing system.

Before each climb, open the gate and let it snap shut. It should close fully and lock on its own without sticking. Look for cracks, sharp edges, grooves worn by rope, and deformation at the nose or hinge. Sap and grit are the usual cause of a lazy gate, so rinse and dry the carabiner and keep the gate mechanism clean.

faq.q: How do you open a Locksafe gate?
faq.a: Twist the sleeve, push it up toward the nose, then open the gate. It relocks when released.

faq.q: Is the Ultra O good with a micro pulley?
faq.a: Yes. The oval shape keeps a pulley centered, which is why it is a common pairing.

That makes it a useful general connector when you want one carabiner style for pulleys, rope grabs, and lanyards. Clip it with the gate facing away from the stem and bark where you can.

Before each climb, open the gate and let it snap shut. It should close fully and lock on its own without sticking. Look for cracks, sharp edges, grooves worn by rope, and deformation at the nose or hinge. Sap and grit are the usual cause of a lazy gate, so rinse and dry the carabiner and keep the gate mechanism clean.

Retire any carabiner that has been dropped from height onto a hard surface, shock loaded, or shows wear you cannot explain. Read the markings on the spine and confirm they meet what your system needs. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers. See more snap hooks.

faq.q: Why use a swivel snap hook?
faq.a: The swivel lets the line turn so lanyards and tethers do not twist up as you move around the tree.

faq.q: Where should I clip it?
faq.a: To compatible hardware such as saddle D-rings. Do not clip it to rope or slings.
